assertions.text: Item operations (add/remove) are represented as their own table or tables — separate from coupon and cart total logic.
Coupon application (entering, replacing, rejecting codes) is represented as its own table — separate from item operations and cart total calculation.
Cart total calculation (how different coupon types affect the price) is represented as its own table — separate from coupon application and item operations.
Checkout (stock verification) is represented as its own table — separate from the other concerns.
Each table row is independently executable — no row depends on a prior row's result. The table expresses rules, not a sequential test script.
Item operations cover at least: add to empty cart, add to non-empty cart, add more of an item already in cart, remove item from cart, remove last item in cart, remove item not in cart.

Coupon application table covers validity and replacement — not coupon types. Scenarios include at least: add valid coupon (none active), add valid coupon (another active), add expired coupon (none active), add expired coupon (another active), add nonexistent code (none active), add nonexistent code (another active).

Cart total table covers how different coupon types affect the price. Scenarios include at least: no coupon, percentage off whole cart, fixed amount off, fixed amount exceeding cart total (floors at zero), product-specific discount (product in cart), product-specific discount (product not in cart).
Checkout table covers at least: empty cart, all items in stock, and not all items in stock (insufficient inventory).
Column names use business/user-perspective language (e.g. 'Message?' not 'Result?', 'Coupon code' not 'input'). The tables read as a specification a product person could review.

Test data that affects the outcome — product prices, coupon rules (type, amount, expiry) — is visible in the table via columns, notes, or explicit setup, not silently hardcoded. The reader can trace how inputs lead to outputs.

Multiple open questions are surfaced — ambiguities or product decisions the requirements don't specify (e.g. what happens to a product-specific coupon when that product is removed, or how percentage and product-specific discounts interact).
Cart totals are arithmetically correct: sum(quantity × price) − coupon = total, for every row in the total calculation table.

Coupon application table uses a column to signal expiry status — either an 'Expired?' yes/no column, a 'Status' column, or equivalent. Expiry is visible per row, not just implied by the scenario name.
Coupon application table uses before/after columns (e.g. 'Active coupon' / 'Active coupon after?') to specify the state change when entering, replacing, or entering invalid coupon codes.
Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Add more of same product', 'Replace active coupon') — not 'Test case 1' or generic labels.

Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.
Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
